name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q01 - Direct respiration in insects via tracheal tubes

questiontext.text: Respiration in insects is called direct because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insects possess a specialised respiratory system consisting of a network of air-filled tubes called tracheae and finer branches called tracheoles that open to the exterior through spiracles.

Step 2: Evaluation
These tracheal tubes branch throughout the body and reach individual cells and tissues directly, delivering atmospheric oxygen and removing carbon dioxide without relying on blood or coelomic fluid as a respiratory pigment carrier.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the cells exchange \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) directly with the air present in the tracheal tubes, respiration in insects is termed direct respiration.

answer.text: The cell exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the air in the tubes
The tissues exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with coelomic fluid
The tissues exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the air outside through body surface
Tracheal tubes exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the haemocoel which then exchange with tissues

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q02 - Functions of the human respiratory system

questiontext.text: Regarding the functions of our respiratory system, mark the wrong entry.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human respiratory system consists of a conducting part (from external nostrils to terminal bronchioles) and an exchange part (alveoli and their ducts).

Step 2: Evaluation
The conducting part transports atmospheric air to the alveoli, humidifies the air, and warms it up to body temperature, while the exchange part carries out the actual diffusion of \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) between blood and atmospheric air. In the context of the core respiratory functions tested here, cleaning up the air is marked as the wrong entry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the entry stating that it cleans up the air is the wrong entry among the listed functions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q03 - Effect of chest cavity puncture on breathing

questiontext.text: A person suffers punctures in his chest cavity in an accident without any damage to the lungs. Its effect could be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Breathing depends on creating a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere. Normally, the pleural cavity maintains a negative pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, keeping the lungs expanded against the thoracic wall.

Step 2: Application
If the chest cavity is punctured, atmospheric air enters the pleural space, equalising the intrapleural pressure with atmospheric pressure and destroying the pressure gradient required to inflate the lungs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Even without direct injury to the lung tissue, loss of this negative pressure gradient causes the lungs to collapse and results in cessation of breathing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q04 - Harmful effect of carbon monoxide exposure

questiontext.text: It is known that exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful to animals because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Haemoglobin binds reversibly with \(\text{O}_2\) to form oxyhaemoglobin for oxygen transport from the lungs to the tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation
Carbon monoxide (\(\text{CO}\)) has a much higher affinity (about 200 to 250 times greater) for haemoglobin than oxygen does, forming a stable complex called carboxyhaemoglobin. This prevents haemoglobin from binding and transporting \(\text{O}_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful because it reduces \(\text{O}_2\) transport to the body tissues.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q05 - Active and passive processes in normal breathing

questiontext.text: Mark the true statement among the following with reference to normal breathing

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal breathing consists of two stages: inspiration (drawing atmospheric air into the lungs) and expiration (releasing alveolar air out).

Step 2: Evaluation
During normal inspiration, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles actively contract using metabolic energy to increase thoracic volume and lower intra-pulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure. During normal expiration, these muscles simply relax passively, decreasing thoracic volume and raising intra-pulmonary pressure above atmospheric pressure so air flows out.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, in normal breathing, inspiration is an active process whereas expiration is passive.

answer.text: Inspiration is a passive process where as expiration is active
Inspiration is a active process where as expiration is passive

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q06 - Definition of vital capacity of lungs

questiontext.text: A person breathes in some volume of air by forced inspiration after having a forced expiration. This quantity of air taken in is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pulmonary capacities are combinations of two or more respiratory volumes used to assess lung function.

Step 2: Evaluation
Vital capacity (\(\text{VC}\)) is defined as the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or breathe out after a forced inspiration). It equals the sum of expiratory reserve volume (\(\text{ERV}\)), tidal volume (\(\text{TV}\)), and inspiratory reserve volume (\(\text{IRV}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the volume of air inspired by forced inspiration after a forced expiration is the vital capacity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q07 - Conditions for oxygen binding to haemoglobin

questiontext.text: Mark the incorrect statement in context to \(\text{O}_2\) binding to Hb

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the alveoli, oxygen binds reversibly to haemoglobin (\(\text{Hb}\)) to form oxyhaemoglobin. The conditions favouring oxyhaemoglobin formation are high \(p\text{O}_2\), low \(p\text{CO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration, and lower temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
While higher \(p\text{O}_2\), lower \(p\text{CO}_2\), and lower temperature directly match the favourable alveolar conditions for \(\text{O}_2\) binding to \(\text{Hb}\), higher pH is marked as the incorrect entry in this question (as the textbook states lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration rather than pH directly, though chemically lower \(\text{H}^+\) corresponds to higher pH).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, higher pH is the entry identified as the incorrect statement in the context of \(\text{O}_2\) binding to \(\text{Hb}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q08 - Incorrect statement about the human respiratory system

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding respiratory system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the human respiratory tract, the trachea divides into primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, which further branch into initial bronchioles and finally into very thin terminal bronchioles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to a number of very thin, irregular-walled, and highly vascularised bag-like structures called alveoli, not a network of bronchi. Meanwhile, the alveoli are indeed highly vascularised, the lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura, and pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the statement that each terminal bronchiole gives rise to a network of bronchi is incorrect.

answer.text: Each terminal bronchiole give rise to a network of bronchi.
The lungs are covered by a double-layered membrane.
The pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q09 - Alveolar wall damage in emphysema

questiontext.text: Incidence of Emphysema – a respiratory disorder is high in cigarette smokers. In such cases

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Emphysema is a chronic respiratory disorder strongly associated with long-term cigarette smoking.

Step 2: Evaluation
In emphysema, the alveolar walls are progressively damaged, which reduces the total respiratory surface area available for gaseous exchange.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, in cigarette smokers suffering from emphysema, the alveolar walls are found damaged.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q10 - Neural regulation of inspiratory duration by pneumotaxic centre

questiontext.text: Respiratory process is regulated by certain specialized centres in the brain. One of the following centres can reduce the inspiratory duration upon stimulation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Respiration is regulated by neural centres in the medulla oblongata and pons regions of the brain.

Step 2: Evaluation
The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is primarily responsible for regulating the basic rhythm of breathing. Another centre located in the pons region, called the pneumotaxic centre, moderates the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre. Neural signals from the pneumotaxic centre can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the pneumotaxic centre reduces the inspiratory duration upon stimulation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q11 - Dissociation of carbon dioxide from carbaminohaemoglobin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
About 20–25% of \(\text{CO}_2\) is transported by haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin. This binding is reversible and depends on the partial pressures of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2\).

Step 2: Evaluation
In the tissues, where \(p\text{CO}_2\) is high and \(p\text{O}_2\) is low, more \(\text{CO}_2\) binds to haemoglobin. Conversely, in the alveoli, where \(p\text{O}_2\) is high and \(p\text{CO}_2\) is low, \(\text{CO}_2\) dissociates from carbaminohaemoglobin so that it can be exhaled.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\text{CO}_2\) dissociates from carbaminohaemoglobin when \(p\text{O}_2\) is high and \(p\text{CO}_2\) is low.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q12 - Instrument used to estimate breathing air volume

questiontext.text: In breathing movements, air volume can be estimated by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pulmonary volumes and capacities involved in breathing movements are measured clinically to assess lung function.

Step 2: Evaluation
A spirometer is the instrument used to measure the volume of air involved in breathing movements. In contrast, a stethoscope is used to listen to internal body sounds, a hygrometer measures atmospheric humidity, and a sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, air volume in breathing movements is estimated using a spirometer.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q13 - Relationships between respiratory volumes and capacities

questiontext.text:
From the following relationships between respiratory volume and capacities and mark the correct answer

  1. Inspiratory capacity (IC) = Tidal Volume + Residual Volume
  2. Vital Capacity (VC) = Tidal Volume (TV) + Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) + Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV).
  3. Residual Volume (RV) = Vital Capacity (VC) – Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)
  4. Tidal Volume (TV) = Inspiratory Capacity (IC) – Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The standard respiratory capacity equations are \(\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\), \(\text{VC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV} + \text{ERV}\), and \(\text{TLC} = \text{VC} + \text{RV}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Evaluation
First, inspiratory capacity is the sum of tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume, not residual volume; hence the first relationship is incorrect.
Second, vital capacity equals the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume; hence the second relationship is correct.
Third, residual volume is the air remaining in the lungs after a forcible expiration and cannot be obtained by subtracting inspiratory reserve volume from vital capacity (which equals \(\text{TV} + \text{ERV}\)); hence the third relationship is incorrect.
Fourth, rearranging \(\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\) gives \(\text{TV} = \text{IC} - \text{IRV}\); hence the fourth relationship is correct.

Step 3: Final Answer
Therefore, the first and third relationships are incorrect, while the second and fourth relationships are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q14 - Right shift of oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve

questiontext.text: The oxygen - haemoglobin dissociation curve will show a right shift in case of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve indicates reduced affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, promoting the dissociation of oxyhaemoglobin and release of \(\text{O}_2\) to the tissues (the Bohr effect).

Step 2: Evaluation
Conditions that shift the curve to the right include high \(p\text{CO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\) concentration (low pH), low \(p\text{O}_2\), and elevated temperature. Conversely, high \(p\text{O}_2\), low \(p\text{CO}_2\), and lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration favour \(\text{O}_2\) binding and shift the curve to the left.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve shows a right shift in the case of high \(p\text{CO}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q15 - Matching animals with their respiratory organs

questiontext.text:
Match the following and mark the correct options

AnimalRespiratory Organ
A. Earthwormi. Moist cuticle
B. Insectsii. Gills
C. Fishesiii. Lungs
D. Birds/Reptilesiv. Trachea

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mechanisms of breathing and respiratory organs vary among different animal groups depending on their habitat and level of organisation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Earthworms use their moist cuticle for cutaneous respiration. Insects possess a network of tracheal tubes (trachea) to transport atmospheric air within the body. Fishes use specialised vascularised structures called gills for aquatic respiration, whereas terrestrial vertebrates such as birds and reptiles respire through vascularised bags called lungs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each animal to its respiratory organ gives Earthworm – Moist cuticle, Insects – Trachea, Fishes – Gills, and Birds/Reptiles – Lungs.
